fields.item_name: Portfolio Layout Patterns for Current Dataset

references.title: User Experience Careers: What a Career in UX Looks Like Today, Second Edition
references.format: Public 90-page research report PDF, with a portfolio-hiring section on pages 74–75
references.access_status: Directly accessible PDF; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: This is the strongest evidence for what a portfolio must communicate. Interviewed hiring managers emphasize clear thought process and workflow, reasons behind decisions, research support, connection to business goals, outcomes, and before-and-after measurement. Those criteria provide a defensible editing standard for selecting and compressing the nine frontend projects.
reusable_patterns: Make the reasoning chain visible: opportunity, evidence, decision, implementation, and outcome.
Tie customer or user value to business or organizational value instead of presenting implementation in isolation.
State which metrics were tracked before and after a change.
Treat the organization and usability of the portfolio itself as evidence of professional judgment.
cautions: The report concerns UX careers broadly, so frontend-specific evidence such as architecture, performance, testing, migration safety, and operational constraints must be added by synthesis.
Quoted hiring preferences are qualitative research findings, not a universal scoring rubric.

references.title: Design a Stand-Out Portfolio for Your UX/UI Niche: UI Design
references.why_relevant: The article supplies a concise reusable case-study structure—problem, role, solution, and outcome—and recommends metrics, user feedback, annotated early artifacts, explicit collaboration, consistent visual design, and uncluttered navigation. This structure maps cleanly onto the current project records and can prevent the nine-project PDF from becoming a screenshot gallery.
reusable_patterns: Open each project with problem, personal role, solution, and outcome.
Include quantitative results or bounded qualitative feedback as proof of impact.
Annotate wireframes, diagrams, or screenshots with the decision they explain.
Describe cross-functional contribution separately from individual ownership.
Keep typography, color, spacing, and navigation consistent across every case.
cautions: The illustrative metrics in the article are examples and must never be reused as if they describe the current projects.
Its web-oriented advice about motion and interaction needs a static print translation.

references.title: Chart Anatomy
references.format: Official design-system guidance for chart structure and labeling
references.access_status: Publicly accessible documentation; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The current dataset includes metrics and diagrams. Carbon defines the functional parts of charts and recommends insight-led titles, concise labels, explicit visual-property meanings, and direct labels where possible. These rules support small, legible A4 evidence graphics rather than decorative dashboard fragments.
reusable_patterns: Write chart titles as qualitative conclusions that state the main insight.
Retain only the axes, ticks, labels, and frame elements needed to interpret the claim.
Prefer direct labels on lines, bars, or nodes over distant legends.
Explain every encoding of color, shape, or size.
cautions: Carbon notes that this chart guidance is a work in progress.
Interactive toolbars, zoom bars, and tooltips are not useful in a static PDF and should be removed or converted to visible annotations.

references.title: Data Visualization Color Palettes
references.format: Official design-system guidance for categorical, monochromatic, and diverging data palettes
references.access_status: Publicly accessible documentation; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The guidance distinguishes palette purpose: monochromatic scales for relationships and trends, and diverging scales for meaningful opposing directions such as rates of change. This supports disciplined use of the Hozui accent palette for before-and-after metrics, architecture emphasis, and project-specific highlights.
reusable_patterns: Use one monochromatic accent scale for magnitude or trend rather than assigning unrelated colors to every metric.
Reserve diverging colors for a genuine semantic opposition such as regression versus improvement.
Keep neutral structure dominant and use accent color only to guide comparison or attention.
Verify that ordered values remain understandable through lightness and labels when printed.
cautions: Carbon palette values should inform behavior, not replace the project's Hozui semantic tokens.
Color cannot be the sole carrier of meaning, especially in grayscale office printing.

references.title: Printing
references.format: Technical guide to print stylesheets, print media queries, and the @page rule
references.access_status: Publicly accessible technical documentation; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The portfolio is generated from web content but must work as an A4 PDF. MDN documents the print-specific stylesheet, print media query, @page sizing and margins, removal of screen-only navigation, and use of higher-resolution imagery. These are direct implementation requirements for reliable export.
reusable_patterns: Maintain a dedicated print layer instead of printing the responsive website unchanged.
Set A4 page size and margins with @page and tune layout within @media print.
Hide controls and navigation that have no printed function.
Use higher-resolution source images for screenshots, posters, and diagrams.
cautions: Browser PDF engines differ in their support for advanced paged-media features, so exports require visual regression checks.
A print stylesheet controls presentation but does not by itself guarantee tagged-PDF semantics or accessible reading order.

references.title: break-inside CSS Property
references.format: Technical reference for fragmentation and page-break control
references.access_status: Publicly accessible technical documentation; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The dataset contains composite evidence units such as metrics, screenshots with captions, video posters, and technical explanations. The break-inside property provides the implementation mechanism for keeping these units intact across A4 page boundaries.
reusable_patterns: Apply break-inside: avoid-page to metric groups, evidence cards, figures, captions, and short comparison tables.
Use break-before or break-after rules deliberately for project openers and major sections.
Allow long prose sections to fragment while protecting the smaller evidence unit inside them.
Test forced breaks together with avoid rules because forced breaks take precedence.
cautions: Avoiding every internal break can create large blank areas or overflow; only protect compact semantic units.
Very tall figures cannot be kept intact on A4 and need cropping, scaling, or subdivision.

references.title: WAI Images Tutorial
references.format: Official accessibility tutorial for informative, decorative, functional, text, grouped, and complex images
references.access_status: Publicly accessible standards guidance; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: The nine projects include screenshots, diagrams, and videos represented by posters. WAI requires alternatives appropriate to each image's function and complete text equivalents for complex graphs and diagrams. The same principle improves PDF comprehension: every visual should have a claim-oriented caption and adjacent explanation that remains meaningful when the image is inaccessible or too small.
reusable_patterns: Caption screenshots with the user-visible behavior or technical decision they prove, not a description of their appearance alone.
Provide a complete adjacent explanation for architecture diagrams and data graphics.
Represent video with a poster, duration or medium label, a concise description of the demonstrated behavior, and a direct evidence link.
Avoid embedding essential prose as pixels inside screenshots.
Treat decorative imagery as optional and give content imagery an explicit informational role.
cautions: The tutorial is written for web accessibility; actual PDF accessibility additionally depends on correct tags, reading order, links, and export tooling.
Alt text alone cannot rescue a diagram whose labels are unreadably small in print.

references.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast
references.format: Official WCAG 2.2 explanatory guidance for graphical-object and interface contrast
references.access_status: Publicly accessible standards guidance; no sign-in required
references.why_relevant: Diagrams, metric graphics, screenshot annotations, and poster overlays must remain interpretable after PDF export and grayscale printing. W3C explains the 3:1 contrast target for essential graphical objects, warns that thin lines can render fainter in practice, and recommends labels, values, borders, or other redundant cues.
reusable_patterns: Keep essential diagram lines, shapes, boundaries, and annotation marks at 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors.
Use labels, values, line styles, or borders so a graphic does not depend on hue alone.
Avoid hairline connectors and pale screenshot callouts that lose visibility after rasterization.
Test the least-contrasting part of gradients and multi-color graphics, not only the nominal token value.
cautions: WCAG's essential exception can apply to authentic screenshots, but accompanying labels and explanatory text should still carry the claim.
Passing a numeric contrast check does not guarantee that a dense or tiny diagram is readable.

strongest_reference.title: User Experience Careers: What a Career in UX Looks Like Today, Second Edition
strongest_reference.selection_reason: It provides the strongest audience-centered basis for the layout: hiring managers want visible reasoning, evidence-backed decisions, business understanding, outcomes, and before-and-after measurement. That gives the nine-project portfolio a selection and hierarchy rule more useful than copying any particular visual style.

visual_patterns: Portfolio grid: use a portrait A4 single reading column with an optional narrow metadata rail; use two columns only for short facts, paired evidence, or before-and-after comparisons.
Portfolio navigation: begin with a nine-row project index showing project number, name, role or period, one-line outcome, and evidence types; mark three featured deep dives and six compact cases.
Project rhythm: give featured projects two to three pages and compact projects one page; keep the same opener, evidence, and outcome positions so readers learn the system once.
Typography: use Hozui SUIT with four stable levels—project title, section heading, body, and caption—and use tabular numerals for metrics where supported.
Color: use a white or Hozui canvas surface, dark default foreground, muted metadata, subtle borders, and one semantic accent; preserve meaning in grayscale.
Hierarchy: place project number and title first, then a one-sentence impact thesis, role and constraints, up to three metrics, and the principal visual.
Metrics: use no more than three large values in one row; pair each with unit, comparator or baseline, timeframe where available, and a source note.
Diagrams: simplify each to one claim, use direct node and connector labels, highlight only the path under discussion, and place a prose equivalent immediately below.
Screenshots: crop to the relevant state, remove decorative device frames, use one dominant image or a labeled before-and-after pair, and add a caption stating what the image proves.
Video posters: use a static 16:9 or source-ratio poster with a restrained play glyph, format or duration label, one-sentence behavior summary, and a visible URL or QR code with a printed fallback.
Tables: use compact two-column mappings for constraint to response, evidence to decision, or before to after; use a three-column project index only when cells remain brief.
Evidence links: group repository, live demo, article, and video links in a consistent footer row; name the destination and evidence type instead of printing raw tracking URLs.
Page furniture: repeat project number, short project name, and page number in a quiet running footer; keep global contact and portfolio URL on the cover and final page.
content_patterns: Curate the nine projects into three featured cases plus six compact cases: feature projects with the strongest combination of measured outcomes, diagrams, implementation depth, and verifiable evidence; keep the rest to one decisive contribution each.
Use one project contract everywhere: context, problem, personal role, team, period, constraints, implementation decision, evidence, outcome, and reflection.
Lead with an impact thesis that names the system change and result, then disclose whether the result is measured, observed, estimated, or qualitative.
Compress technical process into a causal chain: baseline or failure mode, constraint, chosen approach, important implementation detail, verification, and result.
For AI Workflow, Forensic Agent, and other architecture-rich projects, use the diagram to explain boundaries and data flow, then devote prose only to the few choices that show judgment.
For migration projects such as API data transition and TypeScript migration, use a before-and-after structure with rollout safety, compatibility strategy, test evidence, and scope metrics.

For UI and cross-platform projects such as Comma, Kusting, and Geobugirin, show one representative interaction sequence or poster and connect it to user behavior, platform constraints, or delivery outcomes.
For validation and quality projects such as i18n validation, emphasize the defect class, automated guardrail, coverage or failure evidence, and the operational effect rather than showing generic UI.
Separate ownership from team outcomes with explicit verbs: led, implemented, designed, collaborated, reviewed, or inherited.
Pair every metric with provenance: analytics tool, benchmark, test suite, repository history, operational log, or clearly labeled team report; omit numbers that cannot be responsibly explained.
Treat external links as verification paths, not substitutes for the story: the PDF must communicate the claim even when the reader never opens the URL.
Close each project with one changed judgment, accepted tradeoff, limitation, or next validation step to demonstrate reflection instead of presenting every delivery as perfect.
a4_adaptation: Use the existing Hozui SUIT font files from @hozui/tokens and map all text, foreground, canvas, border, and accent colors to Hozui semantic tokens rather than copying Carbon color values.

Create a reusable Hozui-styled ProjectHeader containing Project Badge, title, impact thesis, role, organization, team, period, and Technology ChipGroup; cap the visible technology chips at the few choices relevant to the story.
Create a ProjectIndex table for all nine projects with fixed short cells and a visible Featured or Compact badge; do not place full descriptions in the index.
Reuse the existing metric treatment as a Hozui surface or compact Card with value, label, detail, and provenance note; limit each project opener to the strongest one to three metrics.
Build an EvidenceFigure component for image, diagram, or video poster with a Hozui border and radius, claim-oriented caption, evidence type Badge, and optional link or QR code.
Build a DecisionChain component with four concise steps—constraint, decision, implementation, result—and allow it to render as a row or a vertical stack depending on available page height.
Render video and video-comparison records as selected posters or before-and-after poster pairs; never leave a generic playback control or unexplained thumbnail in the PDF.
Use Hozui Divider or border tokens to separate narrative sections and evidence links; omit web shadows and hover treatments from print.
Set @page to A4 portrait with approximately 16–18 mm side margins and 16–20 mm vertical margins, then verify the usable width against the longest diagrams and project-index cells.
Apply break-inside: avoid-page to ProjectHeader, metric groups, DecisionChain, EvidenceFigure, captions, and short tables; allow long technical explanations to flow naturally between pages.
Use explicit page breaks before featured-project openers and conditional breaks before compact cases only when enough space remains for the opener plus its first evidence unit.
Export screenshots and posters at a print-effective resolution of roughly 150–200 dpi at their placed size; preserve vectors for diagrams wherever the exporter supports them.
Add visible link labels and short destinations beside QR codes so evidence remains reachable when a QR reader is unavailable or the PDF is viewed digitally.
Export selectable text with embedded fonts, descriptive source semantics for figures, functioning hyperlinks, logical reading order, and a final visual check at 100% size and in grayscale.

Use a final two-stage deliverable: a concise core portfolio containing all nine projects and optional linked deep dives for artifact-heavy cases that cannot remain legible within the core page budget.
avoid_patterns: Do not allocate equal page counts to all nine projects; equal treatment hides the strongest evidence and makes the document repetitive.
Avoid a chronological feature inventory. Organize each case around one consequential problem and a small number of decisions.
Avoid technology walls, exhaustive method lists, and responsibility bullets that repeat the résumé without showing evidence.
Avoid tiny screenshot mosaics, full-page device mockups, or uncropped application screens whose meaningful text cannot be read at 100% A4 size.
Avoid inserting a video poster without a caption, demonstrated behavior, and stable evidence link; a play icon alone conveys no portfolio value.
Avoid dense architecture diagrams copied directly from development documentation; simplify them to the boundary, flow, or failure mode discussed on that page.
Avoid pale connector lines, thin chart marks, color-only status, and low-contrast annotation overlays that fail after rasterization or grayscale printing.
Avoid metrics without baseline, unit, period, population, source, or attribution, and never present prototype validation as production impact.
Avoid raw long URLs, tracking parameters, link-only evidence, and QR-only navigation; provide named links and self-contained explanations.
Avoid splitting captions from images, headings from their first content block, metric values from labels, or short decision chains across pages.
Avoid applying break-inside avoidance to every section, which can create large blank regions or overflow on A4.
Avoid printing sticky navigation, hover states, carousels, autoplay behavior, animation, or browser controls; convert them into deliberate static evidence.
Avoid treating Hozui Cards, Badges, and Chips as decoration. Each component should encode a stable content role and remain restrained on paper.
Avoid overlong core PDFs. Move exhaustive logs, galleries, source excerpts, and secondary artifacts into linked project deep dives.
fields.source_quality_notes: The sources were checked on 2026-08-26. Nielsen Norman Group supplies the strongest hiring-research evidence; W3C supplies normative and explanatory accessibility guidance; MDN supplies implementation-level print and fragmentation guidance; IBM Carbon supplies official chart and palette design guidance; Interaction Design Foundation supplies current practitioner-facing portfolio structure guidance. Carbon explicitly labels its chart-anatomy guidance as work in progress. The proposed three-featured-plus-six-compact hierarchy, Hozui mappings, project-specific content assignments, page budgets, image-resolution targets, and component designs are analytical synthesis based on the local nine-project dataset and current portfolio generators, not direct claims from the cited publishers. No source independently verifies the metrics inside the user's project dataset; those values should retain local provenance before publication.
